items.title: Budget-Aware Predict-and-Verify Theorem Proving with Heterogeneous LLM Solvers
items.source_text: Large language model (LLM) theorem solvers differ in both proving capability and inference cost. Applying an expensive solver to every subgoal wastes computation when cheaper models are sufficient, while always starting from the cheapest solver wastes attempts on subgoals that require stronger models. We present BudgetPV, an agentic budget-aware predict-and-verify system that allocates computation across unresolved subgoals and heterogeneous LLM solvers. BudgetPV uses a cross-solver predictor to guide solver selection for each subgoal and revises the allocation as verification feedback…
items.summary: Presents BudgetPV, a budget-aware predict-and-verify system allocating heterogeneous LLM solvers across subgoals in theorem proving.

items.title: Learning Inside Types: Epistemic Typestates for Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.source_text: Type disciplines make programs safe by construction: components checked against each other's types compose into programs that cannot go wrong in the ways the types exclude. Types suit reinforcement learning: a type constrains what an agent may choose, not how it chooses, so the guarantee holds for every policy a learner produces. We introduce epistemic typestates, a type discipline for safe multi-agent reinforcement learning. An agent's type is a protocol whose states record its beliefs, the worlds it cannot rule out from its own observations and actions, and permits only actions that are…
items.summary: Introduces epistemic typestates as a type discipline for safe multi-agent reinforcement learning, not involving formal proofs.

items.title: Compositional Temporal Specifications for Interaction Trees
items.source_text: The correctness of modern effectful programs depends not only on their final results but also on the temporal evolution of observable interactions with their environments. Interaction Trees (ITrees) provide a reusable denotational semantics for such programs by representing effectful computations as potentially infinite trees of observable interactions. However, reusable temporal reasoning over ITrees remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a compositional temporal specification framework for ITrees. We introduce iBuchi, a shallowly embedded temporal specification language based on…
items.summary: Presents iBuchi, a compositional temporal specification language for reasoning about Interaction Trees in effectful programs.

items.title: Verifying and Strengthening Neural Tangent Kernel Theory
items.source_text: Writing Neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory explains why very wide neural networks trained by gradient methods converge in the lazy-training regime. Its standard proof combines matrix concentration, random Gram matrices, continuous-time dynamics, spectral perturbation, and a bootstrap argument, but has lacked machine-checked verification. We present a Lean\~4 formalisation for two-layer networks, proving an end-to-end theorem: for a smooth bounded activation (instantiated with $σ=\tanh$), frozen biases, paired $\pm 1$ initialisation, and explicit width conditions, gradient flow exists…
items.summary: Presents a Lean 4 formalisation of neural tangent kernel convergence theory for two-layer networks with an end-to-end machine-checked theorem.

items.title: Self-verifiable LLM-driven science and why it needs human researchers
items.source_text: Language models are now used throughout all sciences - for reading literature, extracting numbers from tables and spectra, analyzing data, drafting conclusions - and their answers arrive in the same polished confident tone whether they are right or wrong, so a result has to be re-derived by a human researcher before it can be relied on. The cost of that re-checking, not the ability to generate results, is what currently limits AI-assisted research. In the field of mathematics, this problem is solved by proof assistants like Lean 4 and Coq that let any formal statement and its proof be…
items.summary: Argues that LLM-driven science needs human re-checking and contrasts it with proof assistants like Lean 4 and Coq in mathematics.

items.title: Sightline: Calibrated Data-Flow Summaries for LLM-Integrated Applications
items.source_text: Programs increasingly call large language models (LLMs), filling prompt placeholders with program values and consuming the output. Such a call crosses the boundary between natural language and programming language (NL/PL). To follow data across it, an analysis needs a data-flow summary of which placeholders the output uses, but no code describes what the model does. Analyses of these LLM-integrated applications therefore taint every output with every input, creating spurious flows, or ask a second model to label each call, which is costly. We prove, and mechanize in Lean 4, that a…
items.summary: Proves and mechanizes in Lean 4 a data-flow summary approach for calls from programs to LLMs in LLM-integrated applications.

items.title: Tether: Verified Stateful Policy Engine for System-Level Monitoring of Agents
items.source_text: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed for long-running tasks that execute arbitrary shell commands or programs. However, these actions can result in unauthorized network requests or persistent, malicious changes to the user's file system, processes, or privileges. Existing defense mechanisms rely on either LLM-based monitors, which lack provable safety guarantees, or stateless policy enforcement layers, which miss multi-step data flows and execution side-effects unmodeled by the policy language (e.g., network calls initiated inside a Python script). We introduce Tether, a framework…
items.summary: Introduces Tether, a verified stateful policy engine for system-level monitoring of AI agents' shell commands and side effects.

items.title: Formally Verified Semidefinite Programming
items.source_text: We present a formally verified Rust implementation of a first-order semidefinite programming solver, a nontrivial piece of numerical software. We wrote the solver by hand and then directed Claude to generate the entire verification in Verus, an automated theorem prover for Rust programs. We discuss the algorithm underlying the solver, its implementation in Rust, and our pragmatic approach to proving it correct in Verus.
items.summary: Presents a Rust semidefinite programming solver whose full correctness verification in Verus was generated by Claude.

items.title: Isabelle Pool Server: a pooled verification service for prover training and multi-agent proving
items.source_text: Isabelle Pool Server (IPS), a verification service with a pool of warm headless Isabelle sessions behind an HTTP API, with session leasing and reclamation, memory-aware admission control, and a time budget on every call. Its verification interface spans single-step execution, block-level proof checking and whole-theory builds, with checkpoints for cheap branching and backtracking, and a build from scratch as the final arbiter. The service runs as a single container with monitoring and is accessible via a Python client, two MCP servers and a raw HTTP API. In our measurements IPS is level with…
items.summary: Describes Isabelle Pool Server, a pooled HTTP verification service for warm Isabelle sessions supporting proof checking, branching and multi-agent proving.

items.title: A Principled Approach to Concurrency, Nondeterminism, and Asynchrony in Choreographies
items.source_text: Choreographic programming (CP) describes a distributed system as a global program and compiles it into communicating network programs via endpoint projection (EPP). Asynchrony captures the independent progress of communicating processes, while nondeterminism captures the range of behaviours that can arise from their interactions. However, the integration of both features into a theory of CP is absent. We present Nyarlathotep, the first asynchronous nondeterministic CP framework. We define its operational semantics of choreographies and networks using labelled transition systems. Besides…
items.summary: Presents Nyarlathotep, an asynchronous nondeterministic choreographic programming framework with labelled transition system semantics for distributed systems.

items.title: Python Code Generation for Isabelle/HOL
items.source_text: The Isabelle theorem prover provides an environment for formalising mathematics and reasoning about programs. To make verified implementations practically usable, its code generator translates functions expressed in the executable fragment of its logic into conventional programming languages. Its targets have traditionally been functional languages (Standard ML, OCaml, Haskell, and Scala), recently joined by Go. Python, which is becoming the dominant language of scientific computing, data science, and education, has remained out of reach. In this work, we close this gap with a Python backend…
items.summary: Adds a Python backend to the Isabelle/HOL code generator, extending verified implementations to Python for scientific computing and education.

items.title: Path Abstraction for Markov Reward Models: An Isabelle Formalisation in a Free Monoid View
items.source_text: The classical definition of discrete-time Markov chains maps pairs of states to transition probabilities. An alternative, proposed in the context of path abstraction in probabilistic counterexample refinement, is to view them as a transition kernel on the free monoid on the state space, mapping paths directly to path probabilities. In this paper, we first extend the free monoid view and path abstraction algorithm to cumulative rewards on Markov reward models. We then use Isabelle/HOL to formalise Markov chains and reward models in this view, exploiting the discrete finite-prefix semantics to…
items.summary: Formalises Markov chains and reward models in Isabelle/HOL using a free monoid view for path abstraction and cumulative rewards.

items.title: Logical Relations on Display
items.source_text: The metatheory of programming languages suffers from a lack of reuse. Researchers develop individual calculi and prove standard properties, but very few results are truly reused across papers. The problem is worse in proof assistants, where developments routinely duplicate code from prior work or rebuild it from scratch. Category theory provides the most promising path toward reusable programming language semantics. Universal properties capture the type connectives---products, functions, sums---together with their $β$/$η$ laws. Free categorical structures identify syntactic calculi…
items.summary: Argues category theory offers reusable programming language semantics and logical relations for proof assistants, a position on metatheory reuse.

items.title: AuXSpec: Learning to Autoformalize Program Specifications via Executable Postconditions
items.source_text: Formal specifications define intended program behavior and underpin verification, but writing them in theorem provers such as Lean is slow and expertise-intensive, making specification a major bottleneck to scaling formally correct code. Autoformalization from natural-language problems is promising, yet training specification models requires scalable feedback on whether generated specifications capture intended behavior. Prior approaches obtain this feedback through explicit proofs or separately implemented code with formal correspondence proofs, both expensive. We introduce AuXSpec, a Lean…
items.summary: AuXSpec autoformalizes program specifications in Lean using executable postconditions as scalable feedback for training specification models.

items.title: Turing Agent: Agentic Formal Verification for Mathematical Research
items.source_text: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly advancing mathematical discovery, moving beyond benchmark-level problem solving to tackle frontier research problems. This progress is ushering mathematics into an era of proof abundance, raising a fundamental challenge: how can we ensure the correctness of the ever-growing volume of AI-generated proofs and transform them into trustworthy, machine-verified mathematical knowledge? We introduce Turing Agent, an agent harness designed to orchestrate end-to-end formal verification of research-level mathematics. Its wo-scale architecture integrates theorem…
items.summary: Turing Agent orchestrates end-to-end formal verification of research-level mathematics, integrating theorem proving to check AI-generated proofs.

items.source_text: We present CompCert4Lean, a large-scale port of CompCert 3.17's verified compiler core from Rocq to Lean, completed in approximately six weeks by one expert directing parallel LLM agents. Our migration workflow partitions the development along its dependencies, audits translated definitions and theorem statements before large-scale proof reconstruction, and then reconstructs proofs in parallel against stable interfaces. The resulting compiler covers typed CompCert C through x86-64 assembly, discharges all 4,908 recorded proof obligations without project-specific axioms, and produces…
items.summary: CompCert4Lean ports CompCert's verified compiler core from Rocq to Lean in six weeks using parallel LLM agents, discharging all 4,908 proof obligations.

items.title: Learning and Verifying Stabilizing Controllers with Structured Neural Control Lyapunov Functions
items.source_text: This work investigates the joint learning of neural controllers and control Lyapunov functions (CLFs) for nonlinear discrete-time systems. We exploit the structural properties of Input Convex Neural Networks and Polyak-Łojasiewicz Networks to guarantee positive definiteness of CLF candidates by construction, reducing the conditions requiring formal verification. We develop a mixed-integer programming framework to formally verify the remaining stability conditions and introduce an iterative region of attraction (ROA) expansion procedure to enlarge the certified ROA without retraining…
items.summary: Learns neural controllers and control Lyapunov functions with structural guarantees, using mixed-integer programming to formally verify stability conditions.

items.title: Verification-Guided Safety-Repair of Learned Controllers
items.source_text: Formal verification can certify that a learned controller is safe. But what should be done when verification fails? Simply suppressing actions that lead to unsafe next states is insufficient because the dangerous action that ultimately caused the safety violation might have occurred many steps earlier. Retraining modifies the policy globally, thereby potentially introducing new failures. Instead, we introduce ReachECO, a verification-guided repair procedure that exploits the information of failed multi-step reachability analysis for synthesizing explicit constraints on controller behavior…
items.summary: ReachECO uses failed multi-step reachability analysis to synthesize constraints that repair learned controllers for safety.

items.title: MASTA: A Feedback-Scheduled Multi-Agent System for End-to-End Tamarin Modeling and Analysis
items.source_text: Tamarin-based formal verification of security protocols requires expert-authored multiset rewriting rules and temporal-logic lemmas. Translating a natural-language protocol description into a complete formal model with an LLM is hard because syntactic, reachability, and property-level errors compound across the multi-step modeling process, and a single agent that both authors and self-evaluates cannot reliably localize them. We present MASTA, a multi-agent system that addresses these difficulties through three innovations. First, an operational--evaluative role decomposition assigns rule…
items.summary: MASTA is a multi-agent system that turns natural-language protocol descriptions into complete Tamarin models for security protocol verification.

items.title: Partial Borrows in Rust
items.source_text: Rust ensures memory safety by requiring exclusive access to mutably borrowed data. However, a borrow can prevent access to more data than necessary. For example, a method with an &mut self parameter borrows the entire struct, even when the method uses only some of its fields. Calling the method can therefore conflict with an existing borrow of a field the method never uses, causing Rust to reject the program. Resolving such conflicts can require programmers to compromise useful abstractions, make non-local changes to their programs, or worse, resort to unsafe code. We introduce view types, a…
items.summary: Introduces view types for Rust to allow partial borrows, so methods can borrow only the fields they use, reducing borrow conflicts.

items.title: Reusing formal Vlasov-Maxwell proofs to certify plasma solver outputs
items.source_text: AI now produces machine-checked mathematics faster than researchers can read it. Can such theorems do practical computational work? We reuse one from \mbox{OpenAI's} Lean~4 relativistic Vlasov--Maxwell library: initial fields determine the field at an outside point until plasma signals reach it, and the energy leaving a surrounding box before they reach its faces. New Lean proofs and numerical bounds give particle-free references for particle-in-cell simulations across three tasks. Domain size follows analytically from observation time, exposing boundary and initialization errors in WarpX…
items.summary: Reuses a formal Lean 4 relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell library to produce proofs and numerical bounds certifying particle-in-cell plasma simulation references.

items.title: Latency-Preserving Rewrites and Translation Validation for Dynamic Quantum Circuits
items.source_text: A dynamic quantum circuit measures qubits during a run and chooses later operations from the outcomes. These branches make the qubits wait: the outcome must reach the classical controller, and the controller must decide. We present qlin, a compiler that reduces this waiting time. qlin moves operations out of branches without delaying the program, a property proved in Lean 4. For error-correction decoders, which branch on syndromes that are almost always zero, qlin compiles the likely syndromes into one multiway branch and keeps the original program for the rest. A cost model decides when a…
items.summary: qlin is a compiler for dynamic quantum circuits that reduces latency via rewrites, with the latency-preserving property proved in Lean 4.

items.title: Learning from Mutants: Teaching Small Language Models to Synthesise Loop Invariants
items.source_text: Large language models (LLMs) have proven promising for synthesising loop invariants, a long-standing obstacle to automated program verification. Yet, frontier LLMs are typically accessible only through third-party APIs, hampering reproducibility and local deployment. Small language models (SLMs) sidestep these obstacles but require task-specific fine-tuning, for which high-quality training data is needed. We present a failure-driven data curation method for fine-tuning language models to synthesise loop invariants. Inspired by mutation testing, our approach applies semantic mutation…
items.summary: Fine-tunes small language models to synthesise loop invariants for program verification using failure-driven data from semantic mutations.

items.title: Formalizing $\mathsf{einsum}$ with Named Tensor Notation
items.source_text: Einstein notation ($\mathsf{einsum}$) is a widely adopted tensor operation that has proven useful in areas such as machine learning and quantum computing. But it had no formal semantics until recently, and its properties had no mechanized verification. We formalize the denotational semantics of a language of tensors (multi-dimensional arrays) that supports $\mathsf{einsum}$ and repeated tensors ($\mathsf{expand}$). With this semantics, we verify equational rewriting rules about $\mathsf{einsum}$ and $\mathsf{expand}$ that improve the performance of tensor computation. Whereas typical…
items.summary: Formalizes the denotational semantics of einsum-style tensor operations and mechanically verifies rewriting rules that improve tensor performance.

items.title: How rigid is maximum cardinality search? Stability and locality of MCS orderings under edge updates, verified in Lean
items.source_text: For which sets F of edge modifications do a graph G and the modified graph share a maximum cardinality search (MCS) ordering? We prove that they do whenever, along every proper common MCS prefix, each unchosen vertex's neighbour count in the second graph exceeds its count in the first by zero or one. In particular, inserting or deleting any matching, or flipping a single edge, preserves a common ordering, and under the same hypothesis every common MCS prefix extends to a full common ordering without backtracking. Neither part of the hypothesis can simply be dropped: inserting a triangle, a…
items.summary: Proves maximum cardinality search orderings are preserved under certain edge updates, with the results verified in Lean.

items.title: From Pen-and-Paper to Machine-Checked Proofs: Lean for System Identification
items.source_text: Mathematical proofs in scientific papers are often long and intricate, relying on chains of references to earlier results. This makes it difficult for readers and reviewers to verify each and every step. Interactive theorem proving offers a complement: the theorem and its proof are written as code, and every inference is checked by a small, trusted piece of software called the kernel. This paper serves as an introduction to the Lean 4 proof assistant for a system identification and control audience, assuming no prior exposure to formal methods. We first show how a Lean proof is read using…
items.summary: Introduces the Lean 4 proof assistant to a system identification and control audience, showing how Lean proofs are read and checked by the kernel.

items.title: DeCompCert: A Verified Decompiler for CompCert-Generated AArch64
items.source_text: DeCompCert is a Rocq-verified decompiler for AArch64 assembly generated by CompCert. It reconstructs CompCert C through nine reverse passes, combining deductively verified transformations with translation validation. Untrusted OCaml and Datalog analyses propose candidate reconstructions, while verified validators accept only candidates that satisfy the required semantic correspondence. The composed correctness theorem guarantees that every defined, safe behavior of an accepted C reconstruction is matched by the input CompCert assembly; under a safety assumption, the two programs are…
items.summary: DeCompCert is a Rocq-verified decompiler for CompCert-generated AArch64 assembly, combining verified transformations with translation validation.

items.title: C-to-Rust Translation Validation at the LLVM IR Level via AI-Assisted Refinement Proof
items.source_text: Migrating C codebases to Rust is a promising approach to securing legacy software, but existing translators do not guarantee that a translated Rust program preserves the behavior of the C program. Neither rule-based nor large language model (LLM)-based translators have been formally verified, and existing approaches to checking translation correctness are limited to testing and bounded checks, which cannot reason about all possible executions. In this work, we present R2C2, which validates C-to-Rust translation by proving in Rocq that the Rust program refines the C program, i.e., every…
items.summary: R2C2 validates C-to-Rust translation by proving in Rocq that the Rust program refines the C program at the LLVM IR level.

items.title: HOL in HOL: mechanized soundness, completeness and consistency, with and without infinity
items.source_text: What can a logic certify about a copy of itself? For Church's simple theory of types, formalized as a deep embedding in Isabelle/HOL with Henkin semantics and a natural-deduction calculus, the answer has two tiers. On the first tier, plain Isabelle/HOL certifies the logic without an axiom of infinity, by a standard model with one individual. On the second tier, the logic with a Dedekind-style axiom of infinity is certified only in Isabelle/HOL extended by a large enough set-theoretic universe. Both tiers appear in Harrison's self-verification of HOL Light. What the present formalization adds…
items.summary: Mechanizes soundness, completeness and consistency of Church's simple type theory in Isabelle/HOL, with and without an axiom of infinity.

items.title: LLM-Assisted Verification in Dafny
items.source_text: Formal verification of complex algorithms requires expertise in program specification, invariant construction, mathematical proof, and the management of automated theorem provers. Although large language models (LLMs) can generate program code and proof fragments, reliably developing complete machine-checked verifications remains challenging: it requires an iterative process of constructing and validating specifications and invariants, building proofs, diagnosing solver failures, and optimizing verification performance. This paper presents a systematic ten-step workflow for LLM-assisted…

items.title: DafnyCert: Certifying Specification Strength in Dafny
items.source_text: Formally verifying a method with Dafny guarantees correctness relative to its specification. However, a specification may be too permissive, allowing multiple outputs for the same input, even when the implementation produces only one. In this paper, we propose checkable certificates that provide independently verifiable evidence of whether a specification is weak or strong. A certificate of weakness contains an alternative implementation that verifies against the original specification, together with a witness input on which the original and alternative implementations produce different…
items.summary: DafnyCert produces checkable certificates showing whether a Dafny specification is weak or strong, using alternative implementations and witness inputs.

items.title: Pre-QED: Environment Specifications for Agentic Verification
items.source_text: LLM agents are making formal verification practical at scale. Recently, many attempts have raised this as an enticing possibility. However, formal verification at scale is only meaningful if deep formal specifications capturing functionality are available for checking. Unfortunately, recent works seek to bypass this issue by using shallow specifications devised for purposes other than verification. OSS-Verify from Anthropic and Theorem, for example, reuses the fuzz harnesses of open-source libraries as specifications and has an agent prove that each harness never crashes. However, a fuzz…
items.summary: Pre-QED argues agentic formal verification needs deep environment specifications rather than shallow fuzz harnesses reused as specs.

items.title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions: A Proof-Relevant Type Theory for Verified Science
items.source_text: Mathematical proof assistants such as Coq, Agda, and Lean 4 build proof irrelevance into definitional conversion ($p \equiv q$ for $p, q : P$ with $P : Prop$), erasing which derivation established a theorem. While natural for mathematics over fixed axioms, judgmental proof irrelevance is incompatible with verified scientific stores, which must inspect and compare independent derivations of a claim to assess consilience and compute counterfactual retractions when an assay, reagent, or model is invalidated. Moreover, combining definitional proof irrelevance with subsingleton elimination breaks…
items.summary: Proposes a proof-relevant type theory for verified science that keeps distinct derivations of a claim, contrasting with proof irrelevance in Coq, Agda and Lean.

items.title: CFGKAT: A Complete Calculus for Non-Local Control Flow
items.source_text: CFGKAT is an extension of guarded Kleene Algebra with Tests (GKAT) that adds non-local control flow (e.g., break, goto) while maintaining an efficient decision procedure. An axiomatization of equivalence for CFGKAT presents unique barriers created by the presence of non-local control flow and contextual semantics of goto which compromises compositional reasoning. In this paper, we overcome these barriers and present a sound and complete axiomatization of program equivalence in CFGKAT. We verify the loop case of the Erosa-Hendren goto elimination algorithm, a difficult syntactic metatheorem…
items.summary: CFGKAT extends guarded Kleene Algebra with Tests with non-local control flow and gives a sound and complete axiomatization for program equivalence.

items.title: ProofCoder: Continuous Reasoning for Automated Software Verification
items.source_text: Formal verification using proof assistants provides strong correctness guarantees for software, but constructing proofs remains labor-intensive and requires significant expertise. Recent approaches based on large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating proof synthesis. However, these approaches typically constrain the model to a rigid tactic-generation loop, in which the surrounding system controls premise retrieval, proof-state management, and backtracking. We introduce ProofCoder, an agentic proof-synthesis system for Rocq that approaches theorem proving from a coding-agent…
items.summary: ProofCoder is an agentic proof synthesis system for Rocq that approaches theorem proving from a coding-agent perspective.

items.title: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems in Grounded Arithmetic
items.source_text: Reflective Grounded Arithmetic (RGA) is a paracomplete arithmetic in which every term is a program and truth is grounded evaluation. RGA discharges a hypothesis only when it proves the hypothesis decided. This paper shows, in a machine-checked Isabelle/HOL development, how Gödel's incompleteness theorems hold for RGA and for systems built on it. RGA's implication is material and RGA has the disjunction property, so the implications the textbook proof of the second theorem uses fail while its entailments and rules hold: Gödel's proof survives as entailments. RGA does not prove its consistency…
items.summary: Shows Gödel's incompleteness theorems hold in Reflective Grounded Arithmetic, in a machine-checked Isabelle/HOL development.

items.title: Curriculum proof repair with learned counterexamples
items.source_text: Language models (LMs) have substantially lowered the barrier to applying formal verification for building reliable and secure software. Existing approaches commonly follow the verifier-in-the-loop paradigm, but the verifier often provides only coarse, binary pass/fail feedback, which offers little actionable signal on how the proof should be repaired. Recent work shows that counterexamples provide more actionable feedback by grounding proof failures in concrete program states, but generating useful ones at inference time requires costly iterative refinement. We present TopoVerus, an LM-based…
items.summary: TopoVerus is an LM-based proof repair approach using learned counterexamples to give actionable feedback in verifier-in-the-loop formal verification.

items.title: Megrez: A Knowledge-Guided Agent for Formal Mathematics over MK Set Theory
items.source_text: General-purpose coding agents equipped with proof-assistant tools have shown strong performance on standalone competition problems, yet cumulative textbook formalization inside a low-resource mathematical library still faces three obstacles: aligning textbook concepts with library declarations, keeping long-horizon search synchronized with live proof states, and integrating locally verified proofs reliably into a growing codebase. We present Megrez, a knowledge-guided formalization agent for Rocq libraries built on Morse--Kelley (MK) set theory. Megrez coordinates a general coding agent…
items.summary: Megrez is a knowledge-guided agent that formalizes textbook mathematics in a Rocq library built on Morse-Kelley set theory.

The human…

We prove five results: (1) every integer periodic cycle $C \subset \mathbb{N}^+$ of $T$ is a strictly attracting Fatou cycle of $f$ with multiplier $μ_f(C) = 3^{N_{\mathrm{odd}}}/2^N = \prod_{n \in C\text{ odd}} \frac{3n}{3n+1} \in (0,1)$, and $μ_f(O_{1,2}) = μ_F(O_{1,4,2}) = 3/4 1$) isolates $B(O_{1,2})$; (4) on…

items.title: Parametric Proof-Carrying Compilation for Quantum Error-Correction
items.source_text: We present PC-QEC, a proof-carrying compilation framework for quantum error correction parameterized by both code distance and syndrome-extraction scheme. It covers all four schemes---Standard, Flag, Shor and Knill---with circuit-level distance guarantees for every legal code distance in each proved family under the declared error and readout contracts. The circuit-level model permits single-wire Pauli errors at every operation's qubit operands, capturing data errors, readout errors and ancilla errors that propagate into multi-qubit hook errors. For each family and scheme, supplied…
items.summary: PC-QEC is a proof-carrying compilation framework for quantum error correction with circuit-level distance guarantees across four syndrome-extraction schemes.

items.title: Statopia: A Prover--Library Ecosystem for Automated Formalization and Proof Discovery in Statistics
items.source_text: Theoretical results in statistics and machine learning rest on long, technically delicate proofs, and fluent arguments generated by large language models are not necessarily correct. Automated formalization makes such arguments mechanically checkable, and automated proving goes further by discovering machine-checked proofs for statements whose proofs are incomplete or missing altogether. Both require reconstructing assumptions from source materials, accessing specialized mathematical infrastructure and managing long proof developments. We present Statopia, an ecosystem that jointly develops…
items.summary: Statopia is an ecosystem for automated formalization and proof discovery in statistics, combining provers with specialized mathematical libraries.

items.title: SLOT: A model checker for actor-based languages with I/O
items.source_text: In my spare time I has been developing SLOT, a library that can be thought as a formally-verified model checker for functional actor-based languages, performing I/O with nondeterministic side effects (read: Erlang). This project is still at a relatively early stage of development, but recently I’ve achieved the first milestone: completion of the core theory. A little bit about the design choices: I/O is emulated by composable effect handlers. Users can supply their own. This differentiates it from Verdi, which comes with predefined effects related to network and disk (at least when I last…

items.title: Formalization of Filter-Method Construction for Real Numbers in Coq
items.source_text: This paper presents a formalization for a theory of constructing real numbers using concepts related to filters. The formalization is implemented using the Coq proof assistant and is grounded in axiomatic set theory. The theory encompasses various notions such as filters, ultrafilters, principal ultrafilters, and arithmetical ultrafilters. A special filter, namely the non-principal arithmetical ultrafilter, whose existence requires the Continuum Hypothesis to be proven, is employed to establish several non-standard number sets: *N, *Z and *Q. The set of real numbers, R, is subsequently…
items.summary: Coq formalization of constructing real numbers via filters and ultrafilters, grounded in axiomatic set theory and using non-standard number sets.

items.title: LeanDojo-v2: A Comprehensive Library for AI-Assisted Theorem Proving in Lean
items.source_text: Building on recent progress in machine learning for formal theorem proving in Lean, we introduce LeanDojo-v2: an end-to-end framework that unifies repository data extraction, LLM fine-tuning, proof search, AI autocompletion, and LLM-assisted theorem proving in a single software library. In addition, we provide Lean4Code, a lightweight IDE that integrates the various features of LeanDojo-v2 through a simple, mathematician-friendly UI. These tools will enable mathematicians and researchers to easily fine-tune language models on domain-specific Lean codebases and experiment with LLM-assisted…
items.summary: LeanDojo-v2 is a library unifying data extraction, fine-tuning, proof search and autocompletion for Lean, with the Lean4Code IDE.

items.title: LeanContext: Disentangling Mathematical Resources from Local Formal Context in Lean Whole-Proof Generation
items.source_text: Neural theorem proving increasingly uses retrieved premises and project context to support proof generation. Evaluating these resources requires measuring the advantage of target-selected declarations over comparable alternatives and how this advantage depends on training. We introduce LeanContext, a benchmark of 129,826 Lean whole-proof generation problems, to investigate these questions. We group selected complete preceding mathematical declarations as Mathematical Context (MC) and the remaining selected local source commands as Environment Context (EC). Four aligned input views support…

items.title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions
items.source_text: Type theories designed for mathematics or program verification need only that a proposition holds; proof irrelevance in conversion erases, at the kernel level, how a claim was established. A persistent knowledge store, by contrast, must retain that record: who established a claim, by which derivation or external tool, and under which assumptions. This volume presents the theory of Eigenius---a store of typed knowledge over constructive institutions---and develops its metatheory from that requirement. The kernel theory is a dependent type theory with cumulative universes, an impredicative…
items.summary: Develops the theory of Eigenius, a proof-relevant dependent type theory for a persistent store of typed knowledge over constructive institutions.

items.title: SeVerus: Context-Aware, Gamified Benchmarking for Rust Verification
items.source_text: Coding agents achieve high success rates on existing benchmarks for Verus, a verifier for Rust programs. These benchmarks typically provide the auxiliary lemmas needed to complete a proof. In practice, however, such lemmas must be discovered and proved. To capture this challenge, we present SEVERUS, a context-aware technique to generate Verus benchmarks that organizes verification tasks into quests, each divided into levelsin a gamified manner. Using the original proof dependencies in verified projects, SEVERUS constructs one quest per verification target and progressively removes proof…
items.summary: SeVerus generates gamified Verus benchmarks from verified projects by removing proof dependencies progressively to test coding agents.

items.title: When Verification Is Not Agreement: Cross-Agent LLM-to-Dafny Formalization
items.source_text: A verified Dafny postcondition certifies that a formula holds, but it does not guarantee that the result was reached through genuine independent reasoning. We introduce a cross-agent formalization protocol where a Specifier model translates clinical trial criteria into a Dafny predicate, and an Implementer model writes an operational method checked against it. A same-model control establishes that even with no capability gap, independent re-extraction from identical text agrees only 59.3% of the time. Evaluating four model configurations on 96 clinical trial documents, we find that agreement…
items.summary: Cross-agent protocol where one model writes a Dafny predicate from clinical trial criteria and another writes an implementation checked against it.

items.title: Formalising Federer’s Geometric Measure Theory in Rocq — project announcement

items.title: Formalizing inverse problems in the age of AI: possibilities, pitfalls, and an invitation
items.source_text: Proof assistants such as Lean check mathematical proofs down to the axioms, and AI agents have recently made writing such proofs cheap. We describe AutoIP, a Lean library in which classical linear regularization theory, together with the functional analysis it rests on, has been autoformalized by AI agents. A machine-checked proof certifies only the formal statement it proves, so the remaining human task is to confirm that each formal statement says what was intended. We organize the library around this task: a reviewer compares the formal statements with their natural-language counterparts…

items.title: Sundance: A Simple SMT Solver for Program Verification
items.source_text: We present Sundance, an SMT solver for program verification written in about 13,600 lines of Rust. Sundance combines the Cadical SAT solver with congruence closure, linear arithmetic, algebraic datatypes, and pattern-based quantifier instantiation. Sundance produces eDRAT proofs for every unsat answer. On 21,531 queries from Verus, Dafny, and F*, Sundance is comparable to existing solvers, with 26--38 times fewer lines of code than Z3 and cvc5. We further show that its components can be swapped for Z3's arithmetic solver, MiniSat, and the Semper e-graph. We have open sourced Sundance.
items.summary: Sundance is an open-source SMT solver for program verification in Rust that produces eDRAT proofs and matches Z3 and cvc5 on Verus, Dafny and F* queries.

items.title: Verified but Vacuous: Three Failure Surfaces of LLM-Driven Verified Code Generation
items.source_text: What should ``verified'' mean when evaluating LLM-generated code? Many existing pipelines report a single verification number. We argue this collapses three distinct properties measured in a conditional audit sequence: verifier acceptance (Surface A), \emph{syntactic specification binding (Surface B: does the proof obligation bind to the spec?), and \emph{semantic specification fidelity} (Surface C: does the spec capture the informal requirement?). Two empirical demonstrations show the surfaces separate. \textbf{First ($A \neq B$), via Li@Opus (a same-model reproduction of…
items.summary: Argues LLM-driven verified code generation conflates verifier acceptance with specification binding and fidelity, illustrated with empirical demonstrations.

items.title: ProofStudio: Five Proof Assistants in the Browser
items.source_text: Recent advances in AI-assisted proof automation are extending the use of proof assistants in software verification and mathematics. However, greater proof automation does not remove users' responsibility to assess whether formal statements capture their intended requirements, making education in formal specification and reasoning essential. To lower the installation and learning barriers associated with mature proof assistants, we present ProofStudio, a browser-based environment integrating Isabelle/HOL, Lean, Rocq, HOL4, and HOL Light with corresponding worked examples, preconfigured proof…
items.summary: ProofStudio is a browser environment integrating Isabelle/HOL, Lean, Rocq, HOL4 and HOL Light with worked examples for education.

items.title: Friedman--Stanley cofinality without Borel completeness
items.source_text: Friedman and Stanley asked whether an invariant Borel class of countable structures must be Borel complete whenever every countable level of their hierarchy reduces to it. We construct a counterexample in one fixed countable language. The structural counterexample and its principal supporting results have been formalized in Lean~4 and it is available on github.
items.summary: Constructs a counterexample to a Friedman-Stanley question on Borel completeness, with the structural result formalized in Lean 4.

items.title: Math Foundation Formalization Agent: A General-Purpose Approach to Formalizing Mathematical Foundations
items.source_text: Mathematical formalization plays an important role in establishing rigorous and machine-verifiable foundations for mathematical reasoning. With the development of large language models (LLMs) and interactive theorem provers, intelligent agents offer a promising approach to automating the formalization of mathematical theories. This paper presents the Math Foundation Formalization Agent (MFF-Agent), a general-purpose intelligent agent designed to support formalization tasks across multiple mathematical domains. The agent integrates the reasoning capabilities of large language models with the…
items.summary: MFF-Agent is a general-purpose agent combining LLMs with interactive theorem provers to formalize mathematical foundations across domains.

items.title: LARK: Lean-Assisted Reasoning for LLM-Generated GPU Kernels
items.source_text: Efficient GPU kernels are typically low-level and hardware-specific, and LLM agents can now generate them faster than experts can verify. Existing approaches rely on testing, which provides evidence but not a guarantee of correctness. We introduce LARK, an agentic framework that automatically and formally verifies GPU kernels against their PyTorch reference implementations. LARK proves equivalence in functional and memory behavior under exact arithmetic and establishes a new trust boundary: human effort is only needed to verify operator-level Lean semantics ahead of kernel generation time…
items.summary: LARK uses Lean to formally verify LLM-generated GPU kernels against PyTorch reference implementations under exact arithmetic.
